direct_evidence: Lucon's oligarchic argument ties landownership to education, government experience, property interests and Senate supremacy; his speech says those who do not understand law cannot enter the Senate.
comparison_inference: Landownership is framed as a qualification for rule, not merely wealth.
caveat: Political self-justification, not a neutral statute.

direct_evidence: Garios is loved for promising veterans land; soldiers expect training, victory and generous rewards; his so-called people’s assembly is usually made up of soldiers.
comparison_inference: Military reward can become a political constituency; the assembly is not necessarily popular representation.
caveat: Does not prove a universal land-pension system.

direct_evidence: A small estate paid for a cataphract's horse and armor; after conquest the revenue went to a tarkhan, imperial grants were scarce, and the narrator worked as a hired sword hoping to buy land.
comparison_inference: Land revenue sustained expensive military service; dispossession could redirect a soldier into wage labor.
caveat: One character narrative, not a universal cavalry recruitment rule.

direct_evidence: A cataphract's daughter says her archon guardian arranged a marriage to gain the estate; she claimed a horse as legally hers and was sued for theft.
comparison_inference: Guardianship, marriage, property claims and local judicial power can conflict.
caveat: One-sided accusation; no court record or general inheritance rule.

direct_evidence: Pharon's house claims tenant welfare while expecting total loyalty; the political speech says common people create aristocratic wealth and should be protected, but should not manage the estate.
comparison_inference: Paternal protection coexists with unequal control.
caveat: Elite viewpoint; no tenant testimony or lease.

direct_evidence: Apys Varros funds Garios while Garios supplies fame; the narrator doubts land redistribution would prevent Varros from profiting.
comparison_inference: Redistribution can coexist with old capital networks.
caveat: Motive is narratorial inference, not proven corruption.

direct_evidence: A tenant law protects a family paying one-third of its crop, but a landlord allegedly forges a document to evict them; a rebel brotherhood later coerces farmers and the narrator remains in debt to the landlord.
comparison_inference: Formal law can be bypassed; counter-justice can reproduce coercion and old debt.
caveat: Character testimony; not a general Vlandian tenancy statute.

direct_evidence: A man without inheritance substitutes for neighbors in a king's levy; they buy his equipment; after imperial capture he is released on a promise to pay later.
comparison_inference: Community-financed service and post-capture debt complicate land-for-service models.
caveat: Individual case; English irony in 'a most noble gesture' is reflected by Chinese quotation marks around 高尚.

direct_evidence: A family buys land and thralls with raid wealth; the narrator plans to raid overseas and return with silver and slaves to buy land for the family.
comparison_inference: Land accumulation can be financed by raiding and slave-taking.
caveat: Plan and personal account, not evidence of all Sturgian households.

direct_evidence: An orphan says his sister's husband hires a skilled legal advocate and wins the parents' farm before a council.
comparison_inference: Local adjudication exists; legal expertise may affect property outcomes.
caveat: Narrator cannot recount the opposing argument; unfairness is not independently established.

direct_evidence: A fence dispute leads to killing; blood-money is considered, kin violence escalates the deaths, and the narrator cannot afford compensation and flees.
comparison_inference: Customary compensation can fail after violence escalates.
caveat: Criminal's self-justifying narrative; no uniform blood-money tariff established.

direct_evidence: A minor Aserai clan with no fiefs still answers when kin or the Sultan summons it; the narrator seeks fame or land and silver.
comparison_inference: Military obligation can derive from kinship and tribal summons without prior landholding.
caveat: Clan self-description and aspiration, not complete mobilization records.

direct_evidence: A village peddler says steppe tribes trample crops, tax villagers and take men to war; he plans to flee to the Karakhuzaits, who do not answer to the khan.
comparison_inference: Tax, agricultural loss and war compulsion are narrated as linked pressures; alternative affiliation is possible.
caveat: Grievance narrative; do not generalize to all Khuzait society.

direct_evidence: Poros herders have autonomy; livestock rustling and blood feuds are common; the Leonipardes reportedly intervene only when both sides invite arbitration, after which their judgments are obeyed.
comparison_inference: Local authority may depend on invitation and accepted arbitration.
caveat: The English says 'it is said'; single local case, not empire-wide procedure.

direct_evidence: The Eleftheroi descend from runaway slaves and debtors, are valued for frontier knowledge, receive titles and enter retinues, yet remain hostile to imperial authority.
comparison_inference: Military service and local knowledge can incorporate marginal groups without producing full obedience.
caveat: Faction summary; no population figures or detailed legal transition.

direct_evidence: Northwestern residents describe nightly readiness for raids and reject being treated as serfs in safer southern estates.
comparison_inference: Frontier risk can shape local status claims and resistance to uniform dependency labels.
caveat: Personal identity claim; not proof of no dependency.

direct_evidence: Land shortage and war send younger sons to dock work; labor oversupply and gang coercion follow.
comparison_inference: Land loss can redirect households into urban wage labor and expose them to coercive hiring.
caveat: One extreme narrative, not labor-market statistics.
